newsitem.title: USA: Minnesota judge to review tobacco company documents.
newsitem.headline: Minnesota judge to review tobacco company documents.

text.p: A Minnesota judge will review 150,000 pages of sensitive documents U.S. tobacco companies sought to keep confidential, it was reported on Saturday.

"If the tobacco companies had an obligation to disclose the hazards of tobacco products, and this Court concludes they did, their obligation to disclose (these documents) cannot be eliminated by the assertion of attorney-client privilege," the St. Paul Pioneer Press said Ramsey County District Judge Kenneth Fitzpatrick ruled late on Friday.

The judge wrote that a review of the documents was warranted because there was sufficient preliminary evidence of possible fraudulent actions by the tobacco industry in trying to keep the documents confidential.
The tobacco industry has said the documents should remain confidential because they fell under rules governing what can be kept secret between lawyers and clients.

The documents contain research into a possible link between smoking and illnesses. The judge will undertake the review within the next 15 days and will be helped by a specially appointed "master," or assistant, Twin Cities papers reported.
Courts in other states have moved to bring tobacco company documents into the open, but this is the first time a court has issued an order this broad.
"This decision is a monumental step at getting to the truth," Minnesota Attorney General Hubert Humphrey III said in a statement.
The judge will not review all 150,000 pages but will look at representative samples.
The documents include papers provided by the Liggett Group as part of a settlement in March with the attorneys general in the country suing the tobacco companies.
Michael York, an attorney in Washington for Philip Morris, criticized the decision and told the St. Paul newspaper he had never heard of a process like this.
"I frankly don't understand how it can be applied," York said.
